opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we get a lot. I think the biggest difference really comes down to where each company started and what we believed the platform should be built around.

Snowflake started as a cloud data warehouse. It was a really well-engineered system for SQL analytics: you load your data into it, it manages the storage format internally, and you get a nice, easy experience for BI and reporting. That's a great product for that use case, and they did a lot to make warehousing simpler in the cloud.

We came at it from a different direction. Databricks grew out of Apache Spark and the work we did at Berkeley, and from the beginning our users were doing much more than SQL. They were doing data engineering, large-scale ETL, streaming, and especially machine learning. Those workloads need to work directly on large amounts of data in open formats, from many languages, not just SQL. So our core bet was that your data should live in your own cloud storage, in open formats like Delta Lake, Parquet, and now Iceberg, and that lots of different engines and tools should be able to work on that same copy of the data. That's what we call the lakehouse: you get the reliability and performance of a warehouse, with transactions, governance, and fast SQL, but on top of an open data lake that also supports AI and data science natively.

So one difference is openness: open formats, open source, not locking the data inside one proprietary engine. The other is breadth of workloads: we've always treated ML and AI as first-class, not as something added on later. That's become more important over the last few years with generative AI, because companies want to build AI applications on their own data, and that means having governance, data processing, model training and serving, and evaluation all connected in one place.

To be fair, the two have been converging. Snowflake has added support for Python, open table formats, and AI features, and we've invested heavily in data warehousing with Databricks SQL, where we've done well on price-performance. But I'd still say the philosophies differ. One starts from a closed warehouse and opens up over time. The other starts from open data and a general-purpose compute platform and adds warehouse-level performance and simplicity on top. We think the second approach is a better foundation, especially as AI becomes central to how companies use their data.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Snowflake’s internally managed storage with Databricks’ use of open formats such as Delta Lake, Parquet, and Iceberg, and identifies openness as a key difference.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the biggest difference is really philosophical, in terms of where we each started and what we think the data platform should look like.

Snowflake came out of the data warehousing world. They took that model, the SQL warehouse, and did a really good job of building it for the cloud, with separation of storage and compute, and making it very easy to use. But the core abstraction is still a closed, proprietary system where you load your data in and then you can query it with SQL, and the vendor controls the format and the engine.

Databricks came from a very different place. We started with Spark, and the problem we were trying to solve was large-scale data engineering, data science, and machine learning, workloads that don't fit neatly into a SQL warehouse. And a lot of that data was sitting in cheap object storage, in open formats. So the thing we've been pushing is what we call the lakehouse, which is the idea that you keep all your data in open formats, like Delta or Parquet or now increasingly Iceberg, in storage that you own, and then you bring multiple engines to that data. SQL is one of them, but so is Python, so is streaming, so is model training, and so on.

So I'd say the fundamental bets are, one, open versus proprietary formats, and two, whether the platform is designed around one workload, SQL analytics, or around the full range of things people do with data, including AI. We think that over time the AI workloads become the dominant ones, and those really need direct access to the data from arbitrary code, not through a SQL interface.

Now, to be fair, the two companies have been converging. Snowflake has added Python support, they've added Iceberg, they're doing more with AI. And we've invested heavily in SQL performance and ease of use with things like Databricks SQL and serverless. So on the surface the feature lists look more similar every year. But I think the underlying architecture and the incentives still differ, and that shows up in things like how easy it is to use your data with other tools, and how costs behave when you scale up to the really large or really diverse workloads.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly identifies Databricks’ use of open formats and contrasts it with Snowflake’s closed, proprietary system.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is where the two companies started. Snowflake started with a cloud data warehouse, focused on SQL analytics. Databricks started with Spark and a broader set of workloads: data engineering, machine learning, and analytics. So our focus has been on letting you do all of those things on the same data, rather than having separate systems for each one.

Another big difference is the architecture. With the lakehouse approach, the data lives in your cloud storage in open formats, and you can use different tools to access it. We think that’s important because companies are going to want to do things with their data that neither we nor anyone else anticipated.

Obviously, there’s overlap as both platforms expand. But I’d say those are the core differences: the breadth of workloads we started with, and the emphasis on an open data foundation.

r001.rationale: The response says Databricks’ lakehouse stores data in cloud storage using open formats and presents that open data foundation as a core difference.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is where the two companies started and how that shaped the architecture. Snowflake started with a cloud data warehouse, focused on SQL analytics. Databricks came out of Spark and started with the idea that you should be able to do all kinds of computation on your data—data engineering, SQL, machine learning—on one platform.

That led us toward the lakehouse approach: keep the data in open formats in your own cloud storage, and bring those different workloads to it. We think that openness matters because customers want to use multiple tools and retain control over their data.

There’s certainly more overlap as both platforms expand. But I’d say our starting point is a broad platform for working with data and building AI applications, with the warehouse as one important workload within that.

r001.rationale: The response describes Databricks as keeping data in open formats in customers’ cloud storage and presents that as part of its architectural difference from Snowflake.
